lessons.title: From Commit to Cloud: CI/CD Pipelines
lessons.content_md:
# From Commit to Cloud: CI/CD Pipelines 🚦

In the early days, deploying meant someone copying files onto a server late on a Friday night. Modern teams ship many times a day — safely — because a **pipeline** does the boring, error-prone work automatically.

## CI vs CD

| Term | Meaning | Runs on |
|------|---------|---------|
| **Continuous Integration (CI)** | Every change is automatically built and tested | Every push / pull request |
| **Continuous Delivery** | Every passing build is *ready* to release with one click | Main branch |
| **Continuous Deployment** | Every passing build is released automatically | Main branch |

<flipcard front="🔁 What is Continuous Integration?" back="Automatically building and testing every code change as soon as it's pushed, so bugs are caught within minutes instead of at release time."></flipcard>

## A Typical Pipeline

```text
push → lint → unit tests → build Docker image → scan image → push to registry → deploy to staging → smoke test → deploy to production
```

If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and nothing broken reaches users.

## GitHub Actions Example

Save this as `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — GitHub runs it on every push:

```yaml
name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test-and-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest

      - name: Build the Docker image
        run: docker build -t my-app:${{ github.sha }} .
```

Tagging the image with the commit SHA means you always know exactly which code is running.

## Safe Deployment Strategies

| Strategy | How it works | Rollback |
|----------|--------------|----------|
| **Rolling** | Replace servers a few at a time | Roll forward or back gradually |
| **Blue/Green** | Run the new version next to the old, then switch traffic over | Switch traffic back instantly |
| **Canary** | Send a small slice (e.g. 5%) of users to the new version first | Stop the canary if errors rise |

<flipcard front="🐤 What is a canary deployment?" back="Releasing a new version to a small percentage of users first and watching error rates — if it looks healthy, gradually send everyone to it."></flipcard>

## Secrets in Pipelines

Never write passwords or keys in the workflow file. Store them as **encrypted repository secrets** and reference them: `${{ secrets.CLOUD_API_TOKEN }}`.

lessons.title: Observability: Logs, Metrics & Traces
lessons.content_md:
# Observability: Logs, Metrics & Traces 🔭

Once your app is live, you can't attach a debugger to production. **Observability** is your ability to understand what the system is doing from the signals it emits — so you can answer "why is it slow?" at 2 a.m.

## The Three Pillars

| Pillar | What it is | Answers |
|--------|------------|---------|
| **Logs** | Timestamped records of individual events | *What happened* for this request? |
| **Metrics** | Numbers measured over time | *How much / how often*? Is it getting worse? |
| **Traces** | The path of one request across services | *Where* did the time go? |

<flipcard front="🏛️ What are the three pillars of observability?" back="Logs (individual events), metrics (numbers over time) and traces (one request's journey across services)."></flipcard>

## Structured Logs

Plain-text logs are hard to search. **Structured** (JSON) logs can be filtered and counted:

```python
import json, logging, time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("checkout")

start = time.time()
# ... handle the order ...
log.info(json.dumps({
    "event": "order_placed",
    "order_id": "A1042",
    "amount_inr": 1299,
    "duration_ms": round((time.time() - start) * 1000),
}))
```

Never log passwords, tokens or full card numbers.

## Metrics That Matter

For any service, watch the **RED** metrics:

| Metric | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **R**ate | Requests per second |
| **E**rrors | Failed requests per second (or %) |
| **D**uration | How long requests take — watch the 95th/99th percentile, not just the average |

<flipcard front="⏱️ Why watch p95 latency instead of the average?" back="Averages hide the slow tail. p95 means 95% of requests are faster than this — it shows what your unluckiest users actually experience."></flipcard>

## Traces

A single click might travel through an API, a queue, two microservices and a database. A **trace** stitches those steps together so you can see that, for example, 1.8 of the 2 seconds were spent waiting on one slow database query. **OpenTelemetry** is the open standard for producing traces, metrics and logs.

## Tools

| Platform | Built-in observability |
|----------|------------------------|
| AWS | CloudWatch Logs & Metrics, X-Ray |
| GCP | Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Trace |
| Azure | Azure Monitor, Application Insights |
| Open source | Prometheus + Grafana, Loki, Jaeger |
| Error tracking | Sentry |

lessons.title: Alerts, SLOs & Incident Response
lessons.content_md:
# Alerts, SLOs & Incident Response 🚨

Collecting signals is only half the job. You also need to decide **what "good enough" means** and **who gets woken up** when it isn't.

## SLI, SLO, SLA

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|------|---------|---------|
| **SLI** — Service Level *Indicator* | A measurement | % of requests that succeed in < 300 ms |
| **SLO** — Service Level *Objective* | Your internal target for that SLI | 99.9% over 30 days |
| **SLA** — Service Level *Agreement* | A promise to customers, with penalties | 99.5% or customers get credits |

Set the SLO **stricter** than the SLA so you notice problems before you owe anyone money.

<flipcard front="🎯 SLO vs SLA?" back="An SLO is your internal reliability target (e.g. 99.9%). An SLA is a contract with customers that has consequences if you miss it — so it's usually looser than the SLO."></flipcard>

## Error Budgets

A 99.9% monthly SLO allows 0.1% failure — about **43 minutes** of downtime in a 30-day month. That's your **error budget**.

- Budget left? Ship features and take sensible risks.
- Budget used up? Pause risky releases and fix reliability first.

## Alert on Symptoms, Not Causes

| Bad alert | Good alert |
|-----------|------------|
| "CPU above 80% on server 3" | "5% of checkout requests failing for 5 minutes" |
| Fires many times a day and gets ignored | Fires rarely and always means users are hurting |

Every alert should be **actionable**. If nobody needs to act, make it a dashboard, not a page.

## When Things Break: Incident Response

1. **Detect** — an alert fires or users report a problem.
2. **Triage** — how bad is it? Who is affected?
3. **Mitigate first** — roll back, fail over or scale up to *stop the pain*. The root cause can wait.
4. **Communicate** — post status updates regularly.
5. **Resolve and review** — write a **blameless postmortem**: what happened, why, and what changes prevent a repeat.

<flipcard front="🧯 What is a blameless postmortem?" back="An incident write-up focused on how the system and process allowed the failure — not on blaming a person — so people share details honestly and real fixes get made."></flipcard>

Keep a **runbook** for each alert: what it means, what to check first, and how to roll back.

lessons.title: Hands-On: A CI Pipeline for Your Container
lessons.content_md:
# Hands-On: A CI Pipeline for Your Container 🛠️

Let's give the containerised app from Level 4 an automatic pipeline that tests it, builds the image and publishes it to GitHub's container registry.

## 1. A Tiny App With a Test

```text
my-service/
├── app.py
├── test_app.py
├── requirements.txt     # flask, pytest
├── Dockerfile
└── .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

```python
# app.py
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok"}
```

```python
# test_app.py
from app import app

def test_health():
    response = app.test_client().get("/health")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json["status"] == "ok"
```

## 2. The Workflow

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest

  publish:
    needs: test            # only runs if the tests passed
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - run: |
          OWNER=$(echo "${{ github.repository_owner }}" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')   # registry names must be lowercase
          IMAGE=ghcr.io/$OWNER/my-service:${{ github.sha }}
          docker build -t "$IMAGE" .
          docker push "$IMAGE"
```

## 3. Watch It Run

Push to GitHub and open the **Actions** tab. Break the test on purpose (change `"ok"` to `"okay"`) and push again — the `publish` job never runs. That's CI protecting production.

## 4. Challenges

- Add a linting step (`ruff check .`) before the tests.
- Add a status badge for the workflow to your README.
- Deploy the pushed image to a serverless container service (Cloud Run, App Runner or Azure Container Apps).
